sections.title: Guardrails
sections.sub: the router, the input screen and the output guardrail

sets.name: Router
sets.what: Is the first decision right? A short question goes to the quick path, a feature description to the full path, an off-topic or hostile input is rejected.
sets.data: 45 inputs written as a product manager would: 10 questions, 17 feature descriptions, 4 off-topic messages, 7 prompt injections, 7 with personal data; some pairs read alike but must route differently.

metrics.label: route accuracy
metrics.definition: Inputs the router sent the expected way (quick, full or reject), as decided by the app: the classifier, the fallback and the confidence floor.

metrics.label: fallback decided
metrics.definition: Inputs where the classifier did not answer and a fallback decided the route.

sets.name: Input screening
sets.what: Does the screen in front of the models catch what must not reach them: prompt injections, off-topic requests, personal data (which it redacts)?
sets.data: 45 inputs from E1: 7 injections, 7 with personal data (with the number of items to redact), 4 off-topic, 27 clean ones that must not be flagged.

judged.rules: flags and redaction counts equal the expected ones

metrics.label: injections detected
metrics.definition: Planted prompt injections the screen flagged.

metrics.label: personal data detected and redacted
metrics.definition: Inputs with personal data the screen flagged and redacted.

metrics.label: off-topic detected
metrics.definition: Off-topic inputs the screen flagged.

metrics.label: clean inputs wrongly flagged
metrics.definition: Clean inputs wrongly flagged as injection or off-topic.

metrics.label: redaction counts exact
metrics.definition: Inputs with personal data where the number of redacted items equals the number planted.

sets.name: Output guardrail
sets.what: Does the guardrail behind the agent catch a faulty assessment before anyone sees it?
sets.data: 4 assessments with one planted fault each, run through the guardrail alone; deterministic, so a miss is a bug rather than a model result.

judged.rules: the guardrail's action equals the expected one

metrics.label: planted faults caught
metrics.definition: Planted faults on which the guardrail took the expected action (regenerate, or redact).

sections.title: Retrieval
sections.sub: the search tool, the agentic loop and its grader

sets.name: Retrieval
sets.what: Whether the search tool finds the right provisions for a plain-English query, and what the agentic loop (grade the passages, rewrite the query, search again) adds over a single search. Since 3 November the twenty candidate passages are ranked by the cheap model (listwise) rather than by the gateway's reranker, which offers no zero-data-retention endpoint.
sets.data: 20 queries over nine areas of the two regulations, each with the provisions that must be among the five passages returned; every query is run twice, with the loop and with one ungraded search.

judged.rules: the expected provision is among the five passages

metrics.label: must-retrieve recall@5, with the loop
metrics.definition: Share of must-retrieve provisions found among the five passages the agentic loop returned.

metrics.label: must-retrieve recall@5, single search
metrics.definition: The same share for one ungraded search: the baseline the loop is compared with.

metrics.label: what the loop adds
metrics.definition: What the loop adds: the difference between the two recalls, absolute and relative.

metrics.label: searches per query · rewrites
metrics.definition: Searches the loop made per query on average, and query rewrites in all.

metrics.label: nice-to-retrieve recall@5
metrics.definition: Share of nice-to-retrieve provisions found; reported, not scored.

sets.name: Grader
sets.what: Whether the grader that decides 'enough, stop searching' is right: it should say sufficient when a must-retrieve provision is among the passages and not otherwise.
sets.data: Every grade the loop made during the E3 run, compared with the truth of whether a must-retrieve provision was present, together with the confidence the grader gave each one.

judged.rules: the grader's verdict against that same truth

metrics.label: precision of 'sufficient'
metrics.definition: When the grader said 'sufficient', how often a must-retrieve provision really was among the passages.

metrics.label: recall of 'sufficient'
metrics.definition: When a must-retrieve provision was among the passages, how often the grader said 'sufficient'; a miss costs a rewrite, not a wrong answer.
metrics.result: 0.81 (17 of 21; 4 false fails cost a rewrite each)

sets.name: Quick answers
sets.what: The quick path end to end: a short question, one retrieval, a three-sentence answer that must cite the right article, invent nothing, and stay within the passages it was given.
sets.data: 15 questions, one per provision, over the same areas as retrieval; the questions that route quick are scored on what they cite, on invented labels, and on faithfulness judged statement by statement.

judged.rules: citations verified against the corpus, length counted

metrics.label: answered on the quick path
metrics.definition: Questions the router sent down the quick path; only those are scored below.

metrics.label: must-cite recall
metrics.definition: Share of expected provisions the answer cites, at article level, after the guardrail verified the labels.

metrics.label: invented citations
metrics.definition: Labels in the answer that do not exist in the corpus, counted before the guardrail marks them.

metrics.label: faithfulness, mean
metrics.definition: Share of the answer's checkable statements that the retrieved passages (and the organisation facts read) support, judged statement by statement after splitting the text; recommendations and restatements of the input are left out.

metrics.label: within three sentences
metrics.definition: Answers within the three sentences the quick path is asked for.

sets.name: Full assessments
sets.what: The full path end to end: a feature description, the agent's assessment at the DPO's pause, scored on the verdict, the two flags, the citations, the key findings a reviewer expects (by a judge model with a rubric), and faithfulness to the passages and organisation facts it read.
sets.data: 20 feature descriptions over eight areas with expected answers reviewed in two rounds (an AI model acting as the domain expert; the human expert pending), eight confusable pairs among them; five cases were also scored by hand to check the judge.

judged.rules: verdict, flags and citations against the expected ones
judged.judge: key findings with a rubric; faithfulness
judged.human: five cases scored blind to check the judge

metrics.label: high-risk AI flag: missed · wrongly set
metrics.definition: The high-risk AI flag: missed among the cases expected true, and wrongly set among the cases expected false.

metrics.label: DPIA flag: missed · wrongly set
metrics.definition: The DPIA flag: missed among the cases expected true, and wrongly set among the cases expected false.

metrics.label: must-cite recall

metrics.label: key findings matched · partial · missed
metrics.definition: Expected key findings the judge found in the assessment: matched (same point, the expected provision at the asked level or an accepted alternative, the exact severity), partial (same point and severity, provision missing or at the wrong level), missed (point absent, or the severity wrong).

metrics.label: of the missed: wrong severity only
metrics.definition: Of the missed findings, those with the right point and provision and only the wrong severity.

metrics.label: wrong extras
metrics.definition: Findings beyond the expected ones that are legally wrong: a provision cited for something it does not say, an obligation the facts say is already met, a false escalation. Correct extra points are not counted.

metrics.label: red lines crossed
metrics.definition: Red lines no assessment may cross: an invented provision, a claim that something is already recorded, a personal name.

metrics.label: faithfulness of the findings, mean
metrics.definition: As for quick answers, over the findings' text, against the passages the agent retrieved and the organisation facts it read.

metrics.label: confusable pairs both right
metrics.definition: Confusable pairs (two situations that sound alike but have different answers) where both cases got the verdict and the flags right.

metrics.label: judge agrees with a human reader
metrics.definition: The judge's verdicts against a careful non-expert reader's, on five cases scored blind with the same rubric; rows the reader marked unsure are left out.

notes.title: Evaluation report · run of 27 October 2026, retrieval re-run 3 November
notes.headline: The assistant finds the right law and never misses dangerously; where it falls short it puts the right finding one severity step too high or too low.
notes.summary: Routing, screens and the output guardrail are clean. Retrieval meets its target and the agentic loop finds three queries a single search misses. Quick answers cite the right article in 13 of 15 and stay within three sentences. All 20 feature descriptions reached the DPO's pause with an assessment, the high-risk AI flag right every time and no dangerous miss. Where the assistant falls short, it is on the severity of findings it has otherwise got right.

gateway_cost.note: OpenRouter activity page: 27 Oct for E1 E2 E7 E5 E6, 3 Nov for the E3 E4 re-run; the harness prices tokens only, the embeddings are the difference. A first E5 run on the shared retrieval set ($0.32) was superseded by the run on E5's own set; the E3 E4 run of 27 Oct ($0.10, with the Cohere reranker) by the re-run of 3 Nov.

failure_modes.title: Severity one step off
failure_modes.text: All seven wrong verdicts are one step from the expected one, never two and never in the dangerous direction; 7 of the 12 missed findings make the right point with the right provision and only the wrong label.
failure_modes.example: A-001, a recently-viewed strip inside the customer's own account, expected Proceed: "Required: document a lawful basis for recording and displaying viewed products … assess and document the balance before launch (GDPR Art. 6(1), Rec. 47)".
failure_modes.response: Acceptable: the DPO can move a finding one step at the pause, and no verdict was two steps off or in the dangerous direction.

failure_modes.title: Special-category data as a Blocker where a consent route exists
failure_modes.text: Selfie verification with a video-call alternative (A-012) and a doctor's note for a payment holiday (A-017) expected a Required Art. 9(2)(a) finding and got a Blocker: the assistant treats a consent the description does not yet establish as a design fault rather than a condition. A reasonable DPO could read it either way; these rows go to the human expert.
failure_modes.example: A-012, finding 1: "Blocker: do not run it unless customers give valid, informed, specific and freely given explicit consent (GDPR Art. 9(1), 9(2))".
failure_modes.response: Resolved by the human in the loop: the DPO decides whether the consent route exists and lowers the finding to Required.

failure_modes.title: The verdict field milder than the text
failure_modes.text: A-009 and A-020 expected Do not build and got Proceed with conditions, yet both summaries open with a stop. The findings carry the substance; the structured verdict lags the prose.
failure_modes.example: A-020 summary: "Do not implement an unconditional, immediate wipe: erasure rights do not override personal-data retention required by law"; verdict field: Proceed with conditions.
failure_modes.response: Caught by the DPO, who reads the summary beside the verdict field and sets the verdict at the pause; a guardrail rule could catch it earlier.

failure_modes.title: Umbrella article where the paragraph was asked
failure_modes.text: Most of the ten partial findings cite "GDPR Art. 5" for minimisation or storage limitation where 5(1)(c) or 5(1)(e) was expected, or state the fraud carve-out and "not high-risk" without the Annex III citation. The worker's rule "cite the most specific label the tools returned" did not reach these.
failure_modes.example: A-017, findings 3 and 4: minimum proof, retention and erasure, both cited as "GDPR Art. 5".
failure_modes.response: Harmless to the DPO, who sees the point and the article; it costs the partial score only.

failure_modes.title: AI Act Art. 5 is the corpus's weak spot
failure_modes.text: Missed by the single pass in E3 twice, by the loop once, and by both E5 questions that needed it: the article's chunks are long and the recitals that paraphrase it (Rec. 30, Rec. 31) outrank it. A corpus-side fix (shorter chunks, a heading that names the practices) belongs to the embedding and chunking study after the capstone.
failure_modes.example: K-008, social scoring: answered correctly from Rec. 31, without the Art. 5 chunk.
failure_modes.response: A corpus fix: shorter chunks for Art. 5 with a heading that names the practices, so the article outranks the recitals that paraphrase it.

notes.judge_note: The target was written as 17 of 20 on the assumption of 20 scorable rows; with 4 unsure rows left out, 13 of 15 is 0.87 against 0.85. In both disagreements the judge was the more generous reader, so 0.73 matched is if anything slightly generous; the judge was strict in one systematic way, counting a point made only in the summary as absent (A-007 KF1). The unsure rows and the disagreements go to the human expert in round 3.
limitations: One run per case, 20 cases, 15 questions: the numbers locate failure modes, they do not give confidence intervals; a second run would move the verdict count by one or two (A-003 varied 4 to 5 of 5 across four rehearsal runs).

The test data was reviewed by an AI model acting as the domain expert (two rounds); the human expert's review is pending, and the DPIA (A-007, A-009) and Art. 9 severity (A-012, A-017) expectations are the ones most likely to move.
The reviser (E9) and the memory's effect on later assessments are not measured here; pytest and the demo cover the mechanics. The model-dependence run on Mistral Large 4 was not made.

Retrieval (E3, E4) was re-run on 3 November after the reranker changed from Cohere's Rerank 4 Fast to a listwise rerank by the cheap model (the gateway's reranker has no zero-data-retention endpoint, which the deployment's data policy requires): recall with the loop stayed at 19 of 20 and a single search at 16 of 20, with the same misses; the grader's calls improved (precision 1.0, recall 0.81 over 27 grades). The quick answers and full assessments (E5, E6) still carry the numbers of 27 October, measured with the Cohere ranking underneath; a second E3 run the same morning found 20 of 20 with the loop, which is the one-run-per-case caveat in numbers.
next: Nothing in the app was changed in response to these numbers, by the rule set before the run.
A short severity-calibration passage in the worker prompt, one example per severity written from the rubric's definitions rather than from these cases, tested on a fresh set.
Corpus side: the chunking of AI Act Art. 5.
Round 3 with the human expert: the unsure rows, the two disagreements, and the contested expectations (A-007, A-009 DPIA; A-012, A-017 Art. 9; A-010 Art. 22 on an automated hold).
notes.intro: Seven sets, each testing one part of the assistant on its own test data, run once on the models the app ships with. Three sets test the guardrails around the models, two the retrieval of the law, two the whole path from a request to the answer.
notes.data_note: The test data is synthetic: written with an AI assistant in the voice of a product manager, checked by the author, who is not a compliance professional, and reviewed in two rounds by a second AI model acting as the domain expert. A human expert's review is pending, so the expected answers are a careful draft, not a certified reference.
notes.shortfalls_intro: Two of the ten targets were not met, both in the full assessments: verdict accuracy (13 of 20 against 0.80) and key findings matched (59 of 81 against 0.75). Two DPIA flags were also missed. The failure modes below explain them; the first one accounts for most of the gap.
